issues.legal_issue: Property tax rateable value must be assessed under the current municipal statute rather than an inconsistent valuation method preserved under earlier municipal rules.
material_facts: The assessments concerned property tax under the current municipal statute, which provided a method for determining annual rent and rateable value.
The lower court relied on an earlier municipal by-law to assess owner-occupied property, although the current statute contained its own valuation procedure.
The earlier enactment had been repealed, and only by-laws consistent with the current statute were preserved.
issues.conclusion: The earlier by-law could not be used where it was inconsistent with the current statute; rateable value had to be determined under the statute by reference to the rent the property could reasonably be expected to command, subject to the statutory deductions.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 60 and 63 of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994 provide for property-tax assessment and rateable value based on the annual rent at which property might reasonably be expected to be let, less the specified deduction. Section 416(2) preserves earlier by-laws only insofar as they are consistent with the Act; the specific statutory valuation method therefore displaces an inconsistent earlier by-law.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: A party appealed a decision concerning the assessment of property tax.
predicates.current_law_has_specific_rent_valuation_: The law governing the assessment provides a specific method for valuing property by reference to rent it could reasonably command.
predicates.earlier_valuation_rule_conflicts_with_cu: An earlier valuation rule would produce an assessment inconsistent with the method provided by the current law.

issues.definition: When a property-tax assessment appeal involves a specific current rent-valuation method and a conflicting earlier rule, the assessment uses the current method.

issues.legal_issue: For property subject to a sublease and a required payment of part of the sublease rent to the public owner, rateable value is based on the rent retained by the lessee if payment or adjustment of that share is proved.
material_facts: The relevant properties included premises partly occupied by the lessee and partly sublet with government permission.
The lessee was required to pay the government 25% of the gross rent received from the sublessee.
The Court treated the lessee as having only 75% of the sublease rent available to it and made the assessment subject to proof of payment, adjustment, or appropriation of the 25% share.
issues.conclusion: Rateable value for the relevant premises was to be assessed on the basis of 75% of the rent received from the sublessee, subject to proof that the 25% share had been paid, adjusted, or appropriated for the government.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, the relevant measure is the rent the owner might reasonably expect from a hypothetical tenant. Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee explains that actual rent ordinarily provides reliable evidence of that measure unless it is inflated or depressed by extraneous considerations. Where the lessee must pass on a share of sublease rent to the government, the retained amount is the appropriate rental basis, provided the payment or adjustment is proved.

rule.if: property_tax_assessment_appeal and premises_are_sublet and lessee_must_pass_on_rent_share and proof_of_share_payment_or_adjustment_is_produced

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: A party appealed a decision concerning the assessment of property tax.
predicates.premises_are_sublet: The assessed premises, or a portion of them, are let by the lessee to a sublessee.
predicates.lessee_must_pass_on_rent_share: The lessee is required to transfer a share of the sublease rent to the public owner.
predicates.proof_of_share_payment_or_adjustment_is_: The lessee produces proof that the required share was paid, adjusted, or appropriated for the public owner.

issues.definition: Where sublet premises generate rent that the lessee must share with the public owner, and the transfer or adjustment is proved, the rental basis is the amount retained by the lessee.

issues.legal_issue: For self-occupied property that is not sublet, annual rent must be determined by estimating what a hypothetical tenant would reasonably pay under the governing municipal statute.
material_facts: The relevant category consisted of buildings occupied by their owners and not sublet.
No actual rent from a tenant was available for those buildings.
The Court directed the assessing officer to determine the rent a hypothetical tenant would reasonably pay under the current municipal statute.
issues.conclusion: The assessing officer had to determine annual rent by reference to what the owner might reasonably expect to receive from a hypothetical tenant, applying the current municipal statute.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63 of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994 uses the annual rent at which property might reasonably be expected to be let as the basis of rateable value. Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee identifies the rent reasonably obtainable from a hypothetical tenant as the statutory yardstick. India Automobiles Ltd. v. Calcutta Municipal Corporation is also relied on in directing that self-occupied property be assessed on that basis under the governing statute.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: A party appealed a decision concerning the assessment of property tax.
predicates.building_is_self_occupied: The owner occupies the building rather than letting it to a tenant.
predicates.building_is_not_sublet: The building is not let by the owner or lessee to a sublessee.

issues.definition: For a self-occupied building that is not sublet in a property-tax assessment appeal, annual rent is estimated from what a hypothetical tenant would reasonably pay.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory cap based on standard rent cannot limit the assessment where the standard-rent regime is unavailable and no standard rent was fixed for the property.
material_facts: The appellants relied on the statutory proviso limiting rateable value by reference to standard rent fixed under the rent-control law.
The provision governing standard rent had been struck down.
No standard rent had ever been fixed for the properties in question.
issues.conclusion: The standard-rent proviso did not apply to the properties and could not limit their rateable value.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 63(1) of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994 limits rateable value by reference to standard rent fixed under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The Court held that the standard-rent provision had been struck down and, independently, that no standard rent had been fixed for the properties.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: A party appealed a decision concerning the assessment of property tax.
predicates.standard_rent_regime_is_unavailable: The legal regime for fixing standard rent is no longer operative.
predicates.standard_rent_was_never_fixed: No standard rent was fixed for the property being assessed.

issues.definition: When the standard-rent regime is unavailable and no standard rent was fixed, the standard-rent cap does not limit the assessment.
